verdict: Average. 3.7L V6 (Ford Cyclone) with 6-speed auto is mechanically sturdy, but AWD adds a power transfer unit (PTU) and rear driveline that are neglected at 128k, and Lincoln parts/labor run high.
major_issues: AWD PTU/transfer-case seal leaks and PTU fluid never changed (seal ~$950-1,360; PTU replacement $1,500-2,500 typical 100k+). Water pump is internal/behind timing cover on 3.7 (~$1,200+ labor-heavy). Harsh/delayed 6F35 shifts (RepairPal top complaint). Electric power steering recalls; MyLincoln Touch/SYNC glitches; 6-7 NHTSA recalls. Wheel bearings, control-arm bushings on 100k+ cars.
risk_reason: Engine is durable, but at 128k a neglected AWD PTU, water pump or transmission service is plausible and any single Lincoln repair easily crosses $1,000; RepairPal avg $831/yr is already near the budget.
inspect_today: Check PTU/transfer case and rear diff for seepage and burnt-fluid smell; listen for whine/clunk on tight turns; check coolant level/color and any sweet smell or oily pink coolant; cold start for timing-chain rattle; test shifts for harsh 1-2/2-3 or flare; confirm recall completion by VIN (steering); scan for transmission/AWD codes; check for SYNC/touchscreen faults and AC operation.

verdict: Above average overall (RepairPal 3.5-4/5, CR average) and a conventional 6-speed auto rather than a CVT, but the first-year 2016 2.5L turbo carries carbon-buildup, LSPI and a few cracked-head/coolant-leak reports; 140k at auction with unknown history is a gamble.
major_issues: Carbon buildup/low-speed pre-ignition on direct-injected turbo (Mazda TSB/software update; severe engine damage $6,500-11,000 but uncommon). Cracked cylinder head/coolant leak in owner complaints. Turbo oil-dilution (fuel in oil) with short trips. Water pump/coolant leaks, AWD rear diff/transfer case fluid neglect, infotainment glitches, 6-speed shift hesitations, brake/suspension wear on a heavy 3-row.
risk_reason: Typically cheap to run, but at 140k the turbo, AWD fluids and coolant system may be due, and a single engine problem would be catastrophic; as-is purchase with unknown oil-change history raises odds.
inspect_today: Check oil level/color and smell for fuel; inspect coolant reservoir for oil/milky residue and look for white residue at head/water pump; cold start for rattle/rough idle or misfire codes (LSPI); listen for turbo whistle/whine, check for blue smoke on acceleration; check AWD rear diff/PTU leaks; shift quality 1-6; scan codes and TSB/recall status by VIN; check 3rd-row and sunroof/AC function.

verdict: Cheap routine upkeep (RepairPal ~$446/yr, 4/5) but the 2015 (2013-2015 L33) Jatco CVT is a known weak point; at 145k the original unit is on borrowed time and the 84k/7-yr settlement warranty has expired.
major_issues: CVT judder, hesitation, overheating, failure (commonly 60k-130k; replacement $3,000-5,900). Engine oil consumption on some QR25DE, steering rack/EPS, A/C condenser leaks, motor mounts, alternator/AC compressor.
risk_reason: Single largest risk is CVT failure on a 145k-mile 2015 with unknown fluid history; even a replacement/valve-body job exceeds budget. Rest of car is cheap.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid color/smell (burnt/dark, metal fines) if dipstick-accessible; drive for shudder from stop, whine, RPM flare, slip, limp mode, or hesitation at 20-40 mph; scan for P0868/P0744 CVT codes; look for service records or Nissan CVT replacement; check oil level (consumption) and oil leaks; check motor mounts on shift engagement, A/C cold, steering play.

verdict: Strong VQ35DE V6 but paired with a Jatco CVT that sees reports of early failure and belt slip; 185k is the highest mileage in the batch and well beyond typical CVT life with a 2020 that likely had heavy fleet/rideshare use.
major_issues: CVT shudder, belt slip and failure (reports from 64k-130k; replacement $3,500-5,000+). 2020 has factory CVT warranty extension only to 84k/7 yrs, now expired. Also front-end wear (suspension/bushings/control arms), brake wear, infotainment, AC condenser, drivetrain mounts, 12V battery.
risk_reason: 185k with original CVT on a torque-heavy V6; sedan likely high-mileage commuter/fleet. Even routine wear items (control arms, struts, tires/brakes) can push past $1,000.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid condition and service records; test for shudder, slip, whining, delayed engagement and limp mode on acceleration; scan for CVT/transmission codes; check engine for oil leaks and timing-chain rattle; inspect suspension bushings, tie rods, struts; look at tire wear for alignment issues; test AC, infotainment, parking sensors; check for fleet/rideshare history (Carfax).

verdict: Below average at 166k: VQ35DE V6 itself is durable, but the 2015 (Z52) Xtronic CVT is a known judder/failure item and the car is old for the mileage. Web search limit hit for this group; relies partly on prior knowledge rather than fresh sourced data.
major_issues: CVT judder, whine, overheating, failure (typically 90k-150k; $3,500-5,000 replacement; extended-warranty coverage expired). AC condenser/compressor, power-liftgate and electrical faults, front suspension/control arms, exhaust manifold/cat codes, water pump leaks, oil consumption on high-mile VQ.
risk_reason: 166k on the original CVT with no known history; heavy 3.5L SUV and failure of CVT, AC or suspension components each exceed $1,000.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid color/smell and service records; drive for shudder at 20-45 mph, slip, RPM flare, whine; scan for CVT codes; check coolant/oil for cross-contamination, oil leaks at valve covers and front cover; inspect front suspension (clunks, boot tears), AC blows cold, power liftgate, panoramic roof leaks if equipped; check exhaust for rattle/leaks.

verdict: Average (RepairPal 3.5/5, 17th of 26 midsize SUVs; CR average). 2018 Pathfinder is better than 2013-2015 but still uses the Jatco CVT as its main risk; the VQ35DE V6 is generally solid.
major_issues: CVT shudder, slip, delayed shifts and failure (reports 60k-120k; $3,500-9,000 replacement). Towing use accelerates wear. AC compressor/condenser, front suspension wear, brake wear, oil consumption claims on VQ35DE (poorly corroborated), AWD transfer/rear diff service.
risk_reason: 143k is moderate for the VQ35DE, and 2018 CVT is improved, but any CVT trouble on a heavy 3-row SUV costs well over the budget; median chance rather than likely.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid and service history, test for shudder/slip/hesitation and limp mode; scan for CVT/transmission codes; check oil level and consumption signs, leaks; inspect transfer case and rear differential for seepage; check suspension and tires, AC cold, 3rd-row, rear AC, towing hitch wear; verify recall/TSB and CVT warranty extension status by VIN.

verdict: Mixed. QR25DE 2.5L is durable and 2018-2019 CVTs are improved over 2013-2015, with reports from catastrophic failures at ~77-110k up to 265k trouble-free; 120-126k puts both cars in the typical risk window.
major_issues: Jatco CVT judder/slip/failure (reports 77k-110k; replacement $3,500-5,500; fluid service ~$400). Automatic emergency braking false triggers (2017-2018), active grille shutter faults, electrical/infotainment glitches, AC issues, AWD rear diff/coupling service, oil consumption on some units.
risk_reason: Both cars are 120-126k with unknown CVT service; these are mid-risk with improved later-year CVTs, but a CVT issue or AWD service would break the budget.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid condition and service record, drive for shudder/hesitation/whine and limp mode; scan for CVT and ABS/AEB codes; check AWD (rear diff/coupling) leaks and noises; inspect active grille shutter, front suspension, brakes; check AC and infotainment, oil leaks and level; confirm recall (AEB) completion and CVT warranty extension by VIN.

verdict: Cheap to maintain, but 1.8L Jatco CVT has a poor reputation (RepairPal shows failures avg ~64k miles on affected 2007-2019 cars); 2016-2019 are improved, 2015 is the riskiest, and all three cars are past the 84k/7-yr settlement coverage.
major_issues: CVT judder, overheating, whining and failure (typically 60k-130k; $3,000-4,500 replacement). 2015 Sentra: excessive oil consumption reports, A/C failures, steering/suspension wear, motor mounts. 2018-2019: fewer CVT complaints but still the main risk.
risk_reason: All three cars have original CVTs at 127-154k; 2015 (A-006) and the 154k 2018 (A-024) are highest risk, while 2019 (C-027) at 137k is somewhat better. Any CVT failure costs more than the entire budget.
inspect_today: Check CVT fluid condition/service records; test drive for shudder, slip, RPM flare, whine, limp mode; scan for CVT codes (P0868, P17F0, P0746); check oil level/consumption on the 2015; inspect motor mounts, AC cold, front suspension, brake wear; look for fleet/rental history in Carfax; verify recall and CVT warranty extension status by VIN.
